With  tbia  imperfect  survey  of  a  most  interesting  building,  I 
must  bring  to  its  dose  an  Introduction  which  I  fear  has  been 
unduly  extended. 

One  duty  remuins,  however,  to  be  fulfilled,  but  it  ia  always  a 
pleasing  one, — the  acknowledgment  of  obligations  incurred,  and 
kindneasee  received,  during  the  progress  of  the  work.  The 
thanks  of  the  SuRTEES  Society  must  be  gratefully  tendered  to 
Lord  Lanerton  for  his  continuation  of  the  permission  given  by 
the  late  Lord  Carlisle  to  publish  these  selections  from  the 
Naworth  Household  Books,  and  also  for  his  kindness  in  allowing 
Lord  William  Howard's  portrait  to  be  photographed  for  the 
illustration  of  this  book.  My  own  personal  thanks  aa  Editor 
are  due  to  his  Lordship  for  the  courteous  readiness  with  which 
access  to  the  Muniment  BrOom  at  Castle  Howard  has  been 
accorded  to  me. 

The  thanks  of  the  Society  are  also  due  to  Mr.  Woodman,  of 
Stob  Hill,  near  Morpeth,  for  the  loan  of  a  transcript  made  by 
him  many  yeura  ago  of  "  John  Pildrem's  Account- Book,"  then 
in  the  possession  of  Mr.  Luwson  of  Longhirst,  from  which  I 
have  taken  many  extracts.  He  also  placed  in  my  hands 
several  interesting  original  Papers,  which  form  a  valuable 
addition  to  the  Documents  given  in  the  Appendix. 

The  SuKTEES  So<'iETY  has  further  to  acknowledge  with  many 
thanks  the  kind  permission  given  by  Mrs.  Barnes  to  have  a 
photograph  taken  of  the  extremely  interesting  portrait  of  Lady 
Elizabeth  Daere,  which  is  in  her  possession  at  Gilling  Castle. 

The  obligations  I  am  under  to  many  literary  friends,  for 
information  upon  various  points,  will  be  found  acknowledged  in 
the  Notes  in  which  that  information  is  embodied.  But  I  must 
place  on  record  here  my  grateful  sense  of  the  ready  kindness 
with  which  my  inquiries  have  at  all  times  been  answered  by 
them. 

It  would  be  unpardonable  if  I  closed  the  list  of  my  obliga-

tions  without  a  grateful  acknowledgment  of  the  kindness  I

Hon.  Mrs.  George  Howard,  I  shall  always  feel  deeply  indebted 
for  a  most  courteous  reception  and  the  most  kindly  hospitality. 
The  pages  which  follow  give  ample  proof  of  the  exercise  of  that 
gracious  quality  by  their  renowned  ancestor.  It  is  still  a 
characteristic  of  those  who  bear  his  name  and  inhabit  the  stately 
dwelling  which  was  so  long  his  home.

branch  of  the  house  of  Corby.  Elizabeth  Salkeld,  mentioned  above,  was  daughter 
and  co-heir  of  Nicholas  Berdesey,  of  Berdesey,  in  Lancashire,  and  wife  of  Lancelot 
Salkeld,  of  Whitehall.  Her  son  Thomas  sold  his  moiety  of  Corby  to  Lord  William 
Howard,  in  1624.  Lancelot  Salkeld,  of  Whitehall,  states  in  his  Will,  dated  21st 
June,  1610,  that  he  was  lessee  of  the  capital  mesHiiage,  &c.,  of  Over  Couiscliffe,  iu 
the  County  of  Durham,  under  the  Lord  William  Howard,  and  Lady  Elizabeth,  his 
wife,  for  fourteen  years,  and  directs  that  his  wife  should  have  his  interest  in  it  for 
the  first  nine,  and  then  to  pass  to  his  sons,  Nicholas,  Thomas,  and  Lancelot.  He 
leaves  to  "  the  Lady  Elizabeth  Howard  one  beere  cupp  double  guilt  with  a  cover," 
and  to  "  the  right  hon.  William  lord  Howard  one  antient  standing  cupp  double 
guilt  with  a  cover."  His  will  was  proved  at  York,  July  28,  1610.  Thomas 
Salkeld,  doubtless  the  one  mentioned  in  this  will,  was  living  at  Coniscliffe  in  1625, 
in  which  year  he  was  proceeded  against  as  a  dangerous  Popish  recusant. — Cf. 
Sortees'  Hist.  Durham,  vol.  iii.  p.  881.

and  partly  in  that  of  Banipton.  It  was  in  ancient  times  a  large  forest.  Lord

have  made  Tliomthwaite  not  unfrequently  a  place  of  temi>oniry  residence,  probably

attraction  as  regarded  the  chace.  A  ^w  red  deer  still  linger  in  the  wild  solitude  of 
its  hills.  At  that  time  they  must  have  existed  in  great  number,  as  did  also  roe-

Cholmeley  is  given  in  Peacock's  List  of  the  Roman  Catholics  in  the  county  of  York 
in  160-4  : — *'  Secret  marriage.  Richard  Chohnley  Escjuicr  maryed  with  Mary  Hun- 
gate in  the  presence  of  John  Wilson,  William  Martin,  Hugh  Hope  and  ("hristopher 
Danyell  in  a  fell  with  a  popbhe  priest,  as  they  here."  As  Mr.  Peacock  says  in  a 
note,  *'  Here  is  a  record  of  a  picturesque  scene.  The  lady  and  her  lover  dare  not 
marry  in  her  father's  house  for  fear  of  spies,  so  an  appointment  is  made  to  meet  at 
some  secluded  nook  on  the  wild  moorlands ;  a  priest  is  ready,  at  the  risk  of  his  life, 
to  perform  the  rite,  and  the  wedding  party  return  home  without  discovery.  Such 
incidents  must  have  been  very  frequent  during  the  darker  periods  of  the  English 
persecution."

In  person  the  Earl  of  Arundel  is  described  by  Walker  to  have  been  "  tall  of 
stature,  and  of  shape  and  proportion  rather  goodly  than  neat.  His  countenance 
was  majestic  and  grave,  his  visage  long,  his  eyes  large,  black,  and  piercing;  he  had 
a  hrM)ked  nose,  and  some  warts  or  moles  on  his  cheeks ;  his  complexion  was  brown  ; 
his  hair  thin,  both  on  his  head  and  beard.  He  was  of  a  stately  presence  and  g^iit, 
80  that  any  man  that  saw  him,  though  in  never  so  ordinary  a  habit  could  not  but 
conclude  him  to  be  a  great  person,  his  garb  and  fashion  drawing  more  observation 
than  did  the  rich  apparel  of  others,  so  that  it  was  a  common  saying  of  the  late  Earl 
of  Carlisle,  *  Here  comes  the  Earl  of  Arundel  in  his  plain  stuff  and  trunk  hose,  and 
his  beard  in  his  teeth,  that  looks  more  like  a  nobleman  than  any  of  us.*  " — Hist. 
Disc.  221  (quoted  in  Tierney's  Arundel,  p.  487).  The  Earl  died  a*t  Padua,  Sept.  21, 
1&16,  in  the  sixty -second  year  of  his  age,  and  was  buried  at  Arundel.  His  name 
occurs  not  unfrequently  in  these  Household  Hooks.

t  The  Castle  of  Kirkoswald  is  said  to  have  been  originally  founded  in  the  twelfth 
century  by  Randolph  Engayne.    By  the  marriage  of  his  grand-daughter,  Ada,  it 
passed  to  Simon  Morville ;  and  Sir  Hu^i^h  de  Morville,  in  the  2nd  of  King  John, 
obtained  licence  to  fortify  the  castle  and  to  enclose  the  park.    The  possesj^ions  of  the 
llonrilles  descended  to  the  Multons,  by  whom,  in  the  time  of  Edward  II.,  this 
castle  was  further  enlarged  and  fortified.     In  the  7th  of  that  sovereign's  reign,  the 
castle  and  manor  of  Kirkoswald,  the  barony  of  GilsUnd,  and  other  vast  estates, 
passed,  by  the  marriage  of  Margaret,  daughter  and  heiress  of  Thomas  de  Multon,  to 
Balph,  Ix>rd  Dacre,  of  Dacre  Castle.    About  the  year  1500  it  leceived  its  last 
improvements  from  the  famous  Thomas,  Lord  Dacre,  '*  who  encompassed  it  with  a 
large  ditch  for  better  security,  and  beautified  it  at  great  expanse."     When  Lord 
Warden  of  the  Western  llarches,  to  which  he  was  appointed  by  Henry  VIII., 
Thomas,  Ix>rd  Dacre,  frequently  resided  at  Kirkoswald.     Many  of  hid  despatches 
are  dated  there.    On  the  division  of  the  Dacre  possessions  between  the  two  branches 
known  as  the  Dacres  of  the  North  and  the  Dacres  of  the  South,  the  castle  of 
Kirkoswald  fell  to  the  latter  branch,  which  tenuinuted  in  tho  Fiennes  and  Lenuurds. 
By  the  last  of  these,  who  mamed  a  natural  daughter  of  Charles  II.,  and  was 
created  Earl  of  Sussex,  it  was  sold  to  the  Musgraves,  in  whose  possession  it  now 
remains.     The  plan  of  the  cattle  seems  to  have  been  quadrangular,  surrounded  by 
a  moat  which  follows  the  contour  of  the  castle  and  encompasses  it  on  every  side, 
enclosing  a  level  area  of  about  an  acre  and  three  quarters,  nearly  in  the  centre  of 
which  stands  the  fortress.     A  more  detailed  account  of  the  present  state  of  the 
ruins  than  the  limits  of  a  foot-note  will  ndmit  of  will  be  given  in  tho  Appendix, 
taken  from  an  interesting  Pai)er  by  MicliacI  W.  Taylor,  M.l).,  IVnrith,  published 
in  the  Transactions  of  the  Cumberland  and  Westmoreland  Antiquarian  and  ArchuK)- 
logical  Society,  vol.  ii.  part  i.     The  procet^s  of  dismantling  the  castle  was  going  on 
about  the  date  of  this  Household  Book,  and  for  some  time  subsequently.     A  grant 
appears  to  have  been  made,  June  28,  1610,  to  Sir  William  Anstruther,  of  all  the 
materials  of  the  decayed  castle  of  Kirkoswald ;  also  a  lease  of  the  land  on  which  the 
castle  stands,  the  gardens,  &c.  (Dom  :  James  I.  Iv.  51).     The  panelled  roof  of  the 
hall  at  Naworth,  destroyed  in  the  fire  of  18i4,  came  from  Kirkoswnlil,  us  also,  in  all

*  The  northern  name  for  a  blood-hound ;  bo  called  from  its  quality  of  tracing 
the  gleuth,  or  xlot,  a  word  which  signifies  the  scent  left  by  an  animal  of  cliace. 
These  dogs  were  held  in  great  estimation  by  our  ancestors,  particularly  on  the 
Ik>rdcrs,  where  a  tax  was  levied  for  maintaining  them.  Their  scent  was  so  remark- 
ably quick  that  they  could  follow,  with  great  certainty,  the  human  footsteps  to  a 
coniiiderable  distance,  as  foxhounds  chase  a  fox,  or  as  beagles  and  harriers  chase  a 
hare.  Many  of  them  were,  iu  consequence,  kept  in  certain  districts  for  the  purpose 
of  tracing  thieves  and  marauders  through  their  secret  recesses.

*  The  usual  corn  measure  in  the  North.  It  varies  in  different  parts  of  the 
country.  In  some  it  represents  two  bushels,  in  others,  six.  It  is  common  also  in 
Scotland,  where  it  also  varies  in  quantity,  according  to  the  different  sorts  of  grain. 
It  is  a  measure  unktiown  in  the  south  of  England. 

t  Fuel  of  any  kind,  peat,  turf,  wood,  &c.  The  Swedish  langusge  has  eldning^ 
fuel,  from  the  Old  Norse  c/Wr,  the  Suio-Gothic  and  Swedish  eld^  Danish  ild,  Anglo- 
Saxon,  add^  &c.  It  may  probably  admit  of  a  question  w^hether  the  word  be  more 
than  simply  a  contraction  from  a  Scandinavian  compound,  such  as  the  Swedish 
eldlannef  with  the  same  sense. — Cf .  Atkinson's  Cleveland  Glossary,  s.  v. 

The  word  is  still  (not  uucommouly)  used  in  Yorkshire,  and  probably  survives  in 
Cumberland  also.

means  that  my  Lady  was  economical  enough  to  have  her  dress  turned. 

§  So  called  in  contradistinction  to  leather  which  had  been  imperfectly  tanned.  An

persons  using  the  mystery  or  faculty  of  tanning  shall  ofler  or  put  to  sale  any  kind 
of  lesither  which  shall  be  inKufficiently  or  not  thoroughly  tanned,  or  which  shall 
not  then  have  been  after  the  tanning  thereof  well  and  thoroughly  dried,  forfeiture 
is  to  be  made  of  the  whole  hide  if  the  whole  be  insufficiently  tanned  or  dried,  or  so 
much  of  the  hide  shall  be  cut  out  as  may  appear  insufficiently  tanned  or  dried,  by 
triers  appointed  under  the  said  Act.

*  The  only  son  and  heir  of  Thomas  Preston,  of  the  Manor  and  Abhey  of  Furness, 

Esq.,  by daughter  of  ...  .  Westby,  of  Moubrick,  Esq.     Mr.  Thomas 

Preston  died  May  14,  1604,  and  was  buried  at  Heversham.  Mr.  John  Preston 
married  Elizabeth  Holland,  of  Denton,  in  Lancashire.  His  daughter  Margaret 
was  the  first  wife  of  Sir  Francis  Howard. 

The  family  of  Preston  was  originally  seated  at  Preston  Patrick  in  Westmoreland, 
and  came  into  possession  of  the  abbey  of  Furness  by  purchase  from  the  Crown  after 
the  Dissolution.  A  younger  branch  was  settled  at  Holker  in  Cartmel. — Cf.  West's 
Antiq.  of  Furness,  p.  254.

X  Andirons,  i.  e.  moveable  irons,  placed  on  the  hearth  for  the  support  of  the 
wood  or  other  fuel.     The  word  occurs  in  Shakespeare  : — 

" Her  andirons 

were  two  winking  Cupids 

Of  silver,  each  on  one  foot  standing,  nicely 
Depending  on  their  brands." — Ci/mbeline,  Act  ii.  Sc.  4. 

They  were  not  unfrequently  made  of  costly  material,  as  silver,  and  enriched  With 
curious  omumentation.  Andirons  of  this  character  exist  at  Knowle,  and  in  brass 
or  iron  in  other  ancient  mansions.

X  George,  third  Earl  of  Cumberland,  died  in  1605,  and  was  buri^  at  Skipton. 
He  was  a  man  of  great  energy  and  ability,  and  remarkable  for  his  skill  and  know- 
ledge in  the  conduct  of  naval  affairs.  Queen  Elizabeth  held  him  in  high  estima- 
tion, and  made  him  a  Knight  of  the  Qarter.  In  1603,  soon  after  the  arrival  of 
James  I.  in  London,  the  Karl  was  appointed  by  that  monarch  Warden  of  the  Middle 
and  West  Marches  towards  Scotland,  with  the  most  extensive  powers,  and  also 
Lieut.  General  of  the  counties  of  Cumberland,  Northumberland,  and  of  the  town 
and  county  of  Newcastle  upon  Tyne. — See  Ridpath's  Border  History,  p.  705.

•  A  younger  son  of  John  Trevor,  Esq.,  of  Trcvallyn,  Denbighshire.  He  became 
a  Baron  of  the  Kxche(}uer  in  1625.  In  1636  he  uniteil  with  the  rest  of  the  Judges

by  the  ruling  powers.     He  preferred  retiring  into  private  life,  and  died  in  1656. 

f  Sir  Uaudolph  Crewe,  a  lawyer  of  great  distinction.  He  was  born  about  1558, 
and  was  called  to  the  bar  in  1584.  In  1606  he  was  selected  to  defend  the  King's 
title  to  almage,  in  the  House  of  Lords.  Two  years  afterwards  he  acquired  Crewe, 
thus  repossessing  an  ancestral  estate  which  for  300  years  had  not  had  a  possessor  of 
the  name.  He  was  the  builder  of  the  magnificent  mansion  which  is  still  standing. 
In  1614  he  became  Speaker  of  the  House  of  Commons,  and  in  1625  Chief  Justice 
of  the  King's  Bench,  of  which  ofBcc  he  was  deprived  for  denying  the  legality  of 
forced  loans.  He  died  at  Westminster  in  1646,  and  was  buried  at  Barthomley,  in 
u  chapel  which  he  had  erected  in  the  church  there.

t  A  name  justly  reverenced  by  every  English  antiquary.  Sir  Robert  Cotton, 
a  close  and  most  intimate  friend  of  Lord  William  Howard,  was  descended  from  a 
very  ancient  family  which  flourished  as  far  back  as  Edward  IIL's  time  in  the 
county  palatine  of  Chester.  He  was  born  at  Denton,  near  Conington,  in  Hunts., 
Jan.  22,  1570,  and  was  educated  at  Trinity  College,  Cambridge.  He  early  imbibed 
a  taste  for  the  history  and  antiquities  of  his  country ;  a  tnstc  which  was  strength- 
ened by  his  intercourse  with  Joscelin,  Lambard,  Camden,  Noel,  and  other  eminent 
aiitiiiuurics,  who  about  that  time  endeavoured,  though  as  yet  unsuccessfully,  to 
establish  a  society  for  the  investigation  of  British  antiquities.  He  neglected  no 
opportunity  of  acquiring  Chronicles,  Cartularies,  and  other  original  muniments, 
which  after  the  Dissolution  had  got  into  private  hands. 

In  1 599  he  accompanied  Camden  to  the  north,  where  they  jointly  explored  the 
whole  length  of  the  Roman  Wall,  and  brought  away  several  inscriptions  and 
monuments,  which  were  deposited  at  his  seat  at  Conington,  and  afterwards  pre- 
sented to  Trinity  College,  Cambridge,  where  they  still  remain. 

Sir  Robert  was  knighted  on  the  accession  of  James  L  in  1603.  He  was  after- 
wards a  principal  promoter  of  the  plan  for  establishing  the  order  of  baronets,  and 
was  himself  one  of  those  who  were  raised  to  that  rank  at  its  institution  in  1611. 

We  are  indebted  to  an  extraordinary  extent  for  what  we  know  of  the  history 
of  our  country  to  Sir  Robert  Cottou*s  library.  Spelman,  Dugdale,  Strype,  Rymer, 
Hurnctt,  Heurne,  and  others,  have  drawn  copiously  from  its  contents.  Speed  and 
C^undcn  received  assistance  from  it  during  Sir  Robert's  lifetime.  Seldcn  also 
acknowledges  his  obligations  to  him. 

Sir  Robert  Cotton  died  in  1631,  in  his  61st  year,  and  was  succeeded  by  his  son. 
Sir  Thomas  Cotton,  who  married,  as  has  already  been  noticed,  Margaret,  Lord 
William  Howard's  second  daugliter.  Some  Letters  addressed  by  Lord  William 
to  Sir  Robert  Cotton  have  been  preserved  amongst  the  MSS.  of  the  latter.  They 
possess  some  interest,  and  will  be  given  in  the  Appendix.

X  The  episcopal  residence  of  the  Bishops  of  Carlisle,  which,  notwithstanding 
many  alterations,  still  possesses  many  of  its  ancient  features.  In  1300  we  have 
the  first  mention  made  of  Rose.  In  that  year  Edward  I.  spent  some  time  there. 
From  La  Kose  he  issued  writs  for  the  convocation  of  the  parliament  of  Lincoln, 
which,  as  Mr.  Hartshome  states, '*  have  for  ever  associated  the  place,  and  more 
especially  the  name  of  that  monarch,  with  a  defence  of  religious  freedom  that  time 
will  not  obliterate."  Edward  I.  was  no  doubt  either  tenant  or  guest  of  John  de 
Halton.  The  history  of  Rose  really  commences  therefore  with  Bishop  Halton. 
In  the  Stnckland  Tower,  at  the  north-east  comer  of  the  existing  buildingps,  are 
found  the  remains  of  the  ancient  keep.  This  tower  was  probably  built  by  Bishop 
Halton.  In  1322  the  buildings  were  destroyed  by  Robert  Bruce,  and  in  1336 
Bishop  Kirby  had  a  licence  to  crenellate  his  mansion  of  Roos.  He  made  further 
additions,  which  were  continued  by  his  successor.  Bishop  Welton,  about  1356.  The 
general  appearance  of  the  building  at  that  time  probably  much  resembled  Naworth 
Castle.  In  the  15lh  century  the  keep  or  peel  tower  was  restored  or  rebuilt  by 
Bishop  Strickland,  whose  name  it  has  since  borne.  Later  in  the  same  century 
another  tower  was  built  by  Bishop  Bell,  on  the  north  front,  as  shown  by  his 
monogram  on  the  cornice,  which  still  remains.  In  the  16th  century  further 
additions  were  made  by  Bishop  Kite,  who  built  the  tower  on  the  west  side,  which 
bears  his  monogram  and  shield  of  arms,  impaling  those  of  the  Archbishopric  of 
Armagh.  He  is  said  also  to  have  built  the  whole  of  that  side  of  the  quadrangle. 
The  17th  century  witnessed  no  further  additions.  In  1645  it  was  held  for  the 
Royalists  by  Mr.  Lowther,  constable  of  the  castle,  but  was  taken  by  a  party  of 
Col.  Heveringham's  regiment,  and  used  for  some  time  as  a  prison  for  the  Royalists. 
In  1648  it  was  again  garrisoned  by  a  company  of  the  Royalists,  and  after  an 
assault  of  two  hours  was  taken  by  storm,  and  burned  by  order  of  Col.  Cholmley. 
It  wus  sold  afterwards,  along  with  the  manors  of  Dalston  aud  Linstock,  for 
i;il61  lis.  lOt/.  to  Col.  Ileveringham. 

On  the  Restoration  Richard  Sterne  becanic  bishop  of  Carlisle,  aud  regaine<l 
possession  of  Rose,  which  he  partly  rebuilt.  Its  restoration  was  carried  ou  by  his 
successors.  Bishops  Rainbow  and  Smith.  Bishop  Lyttleton  and  his  successors 
made  various  repairs  and  alterations.  Under  Bishop  Percy  the  castle  was  brought 
to  its  present  form,  his  alterations  being  carried  out  from  the  designs  of  Rickman.

•  Sir  William  Selby,  Knt.,  Gentleman  Porter  of  Berwick,  M.P.  1592, 1597, 1601. 

He  succeeded  to  the  estate  of  The  Moat  in  Kent  on  the  death  of  his  uncle  in  1611. 
He  died  at  the  Moat,  without  issue,  Feb.  14, 1637,  and  was  buried  at  Igtham.  Sir 
William  was  son  of  Sir  John  Selby  of  Twisell,  Gentleman  Porter  of  Berwick,  who 
was  knighted  by  Queen  Elizabeth  in  1582.  Sir  William  Selby's  sister  Margaret 
married  Sir  George  Selby,  of  Newcastle,  who  from  the  splendid  hospitality  with 
which  he  entertained  King  James  I.  whenever  he  made  Newcastle  a  resting-place 
on  his  progresses  northwards  was  popularly  denominated  *'  the  king's  host. 

f  In  all  probability  this  was  some  Roman  stone  which  had  been  discovered,  and 
sent  to  Naworth,  by  Mr.  Parson  Cur  wen,  as  an  acceptable  present  to  the  lord  of 
the  castle. 

The  thirty  geese  mentioned  in  the  next  entry  as  sent  by  him  must  clearly  have 
been  a  rent  in  kind. 

t  Possibly  the  wife  of  Robert  Snowden,  who  became  Bishop  of  Carlisle  in  1616. 
He  died  15  May,  1621. 

§  Sir  William  Fenw^ick,  of  Meldon,  Knt.  He  waa  son  of  Sir  William  Fenwick, 
of  Wallington,  by  his  second  marriage  with  Margaret,  daughter  of  Wm.  Selby,  of 
Newcastle,  Esq.  H^  was  knighted  bv  James  1.  in  1616,  at  Cavers  in  Scotland. 
He  was  a  distinguished  loyalist,  and  his  property  was  sequestered  by  Cromwell's 
Parliament  in  1652.  He  died  in  London  the  same  year,  and  was  buried  at  St. 
Andrew's,  Holbom.

f  This  item  refers  to  the  conveyance  of  the  Lordship  of  Plenmeller  to  Lord 
William  Howard  by  Lord  Howard  de  Walden.  In  John  Pildrem's  Account  book 
the  corresponding  item  is  as  follows : — '*  Kcceaved  of  Mr.  Sayere  for  my  I^ord 
Walden's  part  of  the  Fyn  [^fine]  concerning  Plen  Meller  and  others,  vijli.  iiys.,  and 
of  Mr.  Widdrington,  vjli.  vijs.;  so  my  Lord  is  to  pay  all  the  hool  charge,  being 
caste  up  amongst  them,  xiijli.  xjs."  In  1568  both  Plenmeller  and  Uuthank  (in 
the  parish  of  Ualtwhistle)  belonged  to  the  Crown  ;  but  in  1613  they  are  included 
in  a  Grant  to  Theophilus,  Lord  Howard  of  Walden,  in  which  Plenmeller  and  all  iu 
■tone  quarries  are  described  as  of  the  yearly  value  of  £3  6s,  Sd,^  and  Unthank,  then 
in  the  tenure  of  William  Ridley,  worth  20*.  a  year.  The  Inquest  after  Lord 
William's  death  describes  him  as  haWug  holden  of  the  Earl  of  Suffolk,  as  of  hia 
manor  of  Wark,  the  Lordship  of  Plenmeller,  and  the  messuages  and  lands  called 
Plenmeller  township  and  Unthank,  with  the  Lordships  of  Haltwhistle,  Hartlebum, 
and  Byers  Park,  besides  several  other  places  in  the  parish  of  Haltwhistle. — Cf. 
Hodgson's  Hist.  Northumb.  II.  Hi.  p.  343.

*  A  lauxe  U  a  salmon.  It  is  an  old  Norse  and  modem  Icelandic  word,  and  Mr. 
Atkinson  tells  me  he  thinks  it  is  still  in  use  in  some  parts  of  Scotland.  It  is 
common  as  a  prefix  to  place-names  in  Iceland,  Scandinavia,  and  Scotland.  Cum- 
berland was  long  held  by  the  Danes  after  the  invasion  of  Northumbria  by  Halfdene 
in  875,  and  their  occupation  has  left  a  mark,  which  is  still  traceable,  in  many  words 
wliich  yet  linger  on  the  lips  of  the  rural  population,  bearing  witness  to  their  Scan- 
dinavian origin,  and  which  is  especially  noticeable  in  names  of  places.  "Lax.  uu

Howard  and  his  family.  In  1640  there  were  4  men  and  5  women  there,  as  we 
learn  from  the  account  of  w&gea  paid  in  that  year.  Askerton  Castle,  now  used  as  a 
farm-house,  is  a  very  interesting  specimen  of  a  small  Border  fortress.  The  type  of 
the  larger  castles  is  followed  upon  a  lesser  scale.  It  does  not  seem  to  have  g^wn 
out  of  a  pcle  tower,  as  so  many  of  them  did,  but  to  have  been  built  in  its  present 
form  at  one  time,  or  nearly  so.  Two  square  towers  flank  the  central  part  of  the 
building,  which  faces  the  south.  There  is  a  peculiarity  in  the  arrangement  of  these 
towers  which  may  be  most  intelligibly  explained  by  the  diagram  here  ffiven. 

The  angles  formed  respectively 

^^^ at  a  and  b  have  been  contrived 

to  accommodate  the  external 
apertures  of  the  latrines  in  the 
npper  stories  of  each  tower.  The 
initials  T.  D.  on  the  weather- 

moulding  of  the  south- western 

3  tower  seem  to  identify  Thomas, 

Lord  Dacrc,  as  the  builder. 
Behind  is  a  small  quadrangle  with  a  curtain  wall  to  the  east  and  the  stabling  to 
the  north.  Over  the  latter  have  been  apartments,  as  is  shown  by  old  fireplaces 
and  mullioned  windows,  now  walled  up,  but  all  in  their  original  position.  The 
space  is  now  used  us  a  hay-loft.  The  western  side  of  the  little  quadrangle  is 
occupied  by  a  building  attached  to  the  south-western  tower,  which  was  probably 
the  hall.  It  has  a  3-Iight  window  at  its  northern  end,  probably  inserted  by  Lord 
William  Howard.  Each  tower  has  very  small  square  openings  to  the  soutb  for  the 
admission  of  light  and  air,  high  up  in  the  wall.  Similar  openings  occur  in  the 
upper  story  of  the  central  building.  The  other  windows  in  this  portion  are 
modern,  except  a  2-light  mullioned  one  of  16th  century  work.  In  the  apartment 
now  occupied  as  a  kitchen  is  a  wide  arched  fireplace,  on  the  mantle  of  which  is 
carved  in  low  relief  Thomas  Cakleton.  Iuniob.  1576.  In  a  communi- 
cation addressed  to  Lord  Burleigh  in  1592  by  Edward  Aglionby,  concerning  the 
means  of  defence  on  the  Borders,  Thomas  Carleton,  Esq.  is  mentioned  as  bKeing 
'*  Land-serjant  of  Gilsland,"  who,  it  is  stated,  "  ought  to  lye  at  Askerton  Castle."

in  great  favour  with  Queen  Henrietta  Maria.

the  Lady  Margaret  Audley.  A  charter  of  incorporation  was  granted  to  Sackville 
College  July  6,  1631,  Lord  William  Howard  being  a  consenting  party. — S.  P.  Dom.

•  A  Herbal,  under  the  title  of  Paradisus  TerrestrU,  was  pablished  in  this  year 
(1629)  by  Mr.  John  Parkinson,  an  apothecary  of  London,  **  wherein  he  gives  the 
figures  or  all  such  plants  as  are  preserved  in  gardens,  for  the  beautic  of  their 
floures,  for  use  in  meates  or  sauces,  and  also  an  orchard  of  all  trees  bearing  frnit, 
and  such  shrubs  as  for  their  raritie  or  beauty  are  ke])t  in  orchards  and  gardens,  with 
the  ordering,  planting,  and  preserving  of  all  these." — See  Epistle  to  the  Reader, 
prefixed  to  an  edition  of  Gerard's  Herbal  published  in  1633  by  Thomas  Johnson. 
It  is  possible  that  my  Lord  had  bought  this  book  of  Parkinson's.  There  is, 
however,  in  Lord  William's  Library  at  Naworth  the  Seconde  Parte  of  Tumer^t 
Herbal  (by  Arnold  Birckmau  in  the  yeare  of  our  Lord  M.D.),  Collon,  1562. 

t  Although  this  is  called  the  Household-book  for  1629,  it  contains  many  entries 
for  1630,  beginning  as  it  does  Nov.  5,  in  the  year  preceding.  This  entry  therefore 
for  u  mourning  suit  corresponds  with  the  time  of  the  Dowager  Countess  of  Arun- 
del's  decease,  which  took  place  April  13th,  1630.  From  a  subsequent  entry  in 
these  Accounts  we  find  that  the  outward  signs  of  mourning  were  not  then  confined 
to  the  person  of  one  who  bad  lost  a  near  relative,  but  extended  also  to  the  trap- 
pings of  the  horse  which  he  rode.  My  Lord  had  his  saddle  covered  with  black 
cloth,  and  a  black  bridle,  crupper,  and  girths.  "  Black  riding  furniture  **  was  also 
got  for  my  I^ady.

*  Amongst  the  rnnny  names  given  to  Plumbi  Suhcarhoncu,  or  sub-carbonate  of 
lead,  occurs  Magistrum  Plumbi.  It  is  used  in  the  formation  of  ointments  and 
plasters. — Cf.  Dunglison's  Diet,  of  Med.  Science,  p.  686.  The  same  writer  explains 
the  term  Magistral  or  Magistralit  as  extemporaneous,  medicines  being  so  called 
which  are  prepared  extemporaneously,  officinal  being  such  as  have  been  prepared 
for  some  time  before  they  are  used. 

t  Judge  Doddridge  composed  a  variety  of  works,  legal  and  antiquarian,  none  of 
which  were  published  in  bis  lifetime,  though  it  is  pro^ble  that  some  of  them  may 
have  been  either  privately  printed  or  manuscript  copies  given  to  his  friends.  This 
'*  book  of  Judge  Dudaridge's  his  mukeinge"  whs  in  all  likelihood  2^A«  Zairyer'f 
Light  :  or  Due  Direction  for  thn  Study  of  the  Law,  which  was  published  in  qiiurto 
in  1629.  He  was  a  very  eminent  lawyer,  and  became  a  Judge  of  the  King's 
Bench  in  1612.  He  argued  the  famous  case  of  the  Post  nati  (State  Trials,  ii.  56i5). 
History  was  a  favourite  study  of  his,  and  he  was  one  of  the  earliest  members  of  the 
{Society  of  Antiquaries,  which  was  dissolved  by  James  I.'s  suspicious  fears.  The 
Judge  died  Sept.  13,  1628,  and  was  buried  in  the  Lady  chapel  of  Exeter  Cathedral,

*  Arundel  House  was  one  of  those  great  mansions  belonging  to  the  higher 
nobility,  whose  size  admitted  of  more  thnn  one  household,  so  to  speak,  being  acconi* 
modated  witiiiu  their  precincts.  Lord  William,  as  we  see,  had  his  "  lodgings,"  or 
suite  of  apartments  for  himself  and  his  domestics  within  the  town  palace  (for  such 
it  was)  of  the  Earls  of  ArundeL  The  great  ecclesiastics  had  similar  town  houses. 
York  house,  Durham  house,  Ely  house,  will  readily  occur  to  the  memory.  Dur- 
ham house  (wiiich,  as  well  as  Arundel  house,  was  in  the  Strand)  "  was  large 
enough,"  says  Heylin,  *<to  allow  sufficient  quarters  for  Buckridge,  Bishop  of 
Rochester,  and  Laud,  Dean  of  Gloucester,  which  he  enjoyed  when  he  was  Bishop  of 
St.  David's  also." — Cyp.  Angl.  p.  69.  Lambeth  Palace  still  survives  to  give  some 
idea  of  what  these  stately  old  mansions  were  in  the  16th  and  17th  centuries.  The 
Due  de  Sully,  who  was  lodged  in  Arundel  house  during  his  embassy  to  England  on 
the  accession  of  James  I.,  says  that  it  was  one  of  the  finest  and  most  commodious 
of  any  in  London  from  its  great  number  of  apartments  on  the  same  floor.  It  was 
taken  down  towards  the  latter  part  of  the  17th  century,  but  the  family  name  and 
titles  are  retained  in  the  streets  which  rose  on  its  siu%  viz.,  Howanl,  Norfolk, 
Aruudcl,  and  Surrey. — Cf.  Pennant's  Loudon,  p.  158  (3rd  cd.  1793;.

*  This  is  an  uncoiumoii  word,  bat  was  in  ase  in  Westmoreland  and  in  West 
Cumberland  some  forty  or  fifty  years  af^,  and  is  still  employed  in  the  Lothians, 
Scotland ;  and  means  as  much  land  as  one  yoke  of  oxen  could  conveniently  plough 
and  cultivate  in  one  year.  It  is  equivalent)  to  the  well-known  term  bovate,  or 
oxgang.  The  extent  differed  in  different  locidities,  owing,  doubtless,  to  the  nature 
of  the  soil.  In  Boldon  Buke  it  varies  from  eight  acres  to  twenty.  In  a  charter 
of  Reginald  de  Wynterse,  giving  land  at  Little  Staynton  to  the  Prior  and  monks  of 
Finchale,  we  find  a  bovate  of  land  described  as  consisting  of  the  definite  number  of 
thirty  acres. — Cf.  Priory  of  Firichale  (pub.  Surtees  Soc.),  p.  69.  In  some  districts, 
no  doubt,  the  quantity  comprised  under  the  term  was  greater  ;  as  much,  perhaps, 
as  sixty  or  eighty  acres.  I  am  indebted  for  information  as  to  the  ase  of  this  word 
to  the  Kev.  C.  B.  Norcliflc.

The  Burrough  of  Morpeth. — December  6.  Rec.  of 
William   Greene   and  John    Pye,   Bailifies   of    Morpeth,   for 

*  Eldest  son  of  Sir  Henry  Widdrington,  of  Swinburne  Castle,  Knt.  He  was 
created  Lord  Widdrington  19th  Charles  I.  He  was  "  a  man,"  says  Echard,  **  of 
singular  courage  and  bravery,  and  as  great  and  graceful  in  his  person  as  any  in  the 
nation ;  much  exalted  by  nature  above  the  tallest  men  of  the  ago  :  of  a  very  fair 
fortune ;  of  which  he  expended  thirty-five  thousand  pounds  in  the  service  of  the 
King." — Hist.  Engl.  ii.  p.  709.  He  was  one  of  Charles'  most  energetic  adherents, 
and  lost  his  life  in  the  Royal  cause  near  Wigau,  in  an  engagement  with  Col. 
Lilburn's  forces. 

t  It  is  not  improbable  that  Mr.  Simon  Musgrave  may  have  been  a  son  of 
Thomas  Musgrave,  Captain  of  Bewcastle,  who  was  the  second  son  of  Sir 
Simon  Musgrave,  Knt.,  who  in  the  11th  Eliz.  was  Sheriff  of  Cumberland. 
Thomas  Musgrave,  was  twice  married,  his  first  wife  being  Ursula,  daughter  and 
co-heir  of  Sir  Reginald  Curnaby  and  widow  of  Sir  Edward  Widdrington.  His 
second  wife  was  a  Scotch  woman. — Cf.  Nicholson  and  Burn,  i.  p.  595,  who  give  no 
account,  however,  of  the  issue  of  either  marriage.

*  During  the  middle  ages  dwarfs  shared  with  fools  the  favoar  of  courts  and  of 
the  nobility,  and  they  maintained  their  place  amongst  the  retainers  in  great  houses 
do\vn  to  this  period.  The  celebrated  dwarf  Geoffrey  Hudson  was  page  to  Queen 
Henrietta  Maria.  Charles  I.  honoured  with  his  presence  the  marriage  of  two 
dwarfs,  Richard  Gibson  and  Ann  Shepherd.  Waller  wrote  a  poem  on  the  occasion, 
and  Sir  Peter  Lely  painted  the  couple  at  full  length.  Gibson  rose  to  some  celebrity 
us  a  painter.  Lady  Arundel's  dwarf  seems  to  have  been  a  favourite  attendant.  A 
letter  (dated  July  17,  1620)  from  an  Italian  agent  of  Lord  Arundel  mentions 
Rubens  having  made  a  sketch  of  the  Countess,  with  Robin  the  dwarfs  the  fool,  and 
the  dog.  The  letter,  which  is  somewhat  interesting,  is  in  the  possession  of  the 
Duke  of  Norfolk.  By  his  courteous  permission  I  am  enabled  to  give  a  copy  of  it, 
which  will  appear  in  the  Appendix. 

There  is  a  curious  portrait  at  Muncaster  Castle,  in  Cumberland,  of  Thomas 
Skeltoii,  who  was  a  domestic  fool  in  the  Pennington  family  about  the  time  of  the 
civil  wars. — Cf.  Lysons*  Magna  BrUanniat  iv.  p.  140.

Nicholson  and  Bum,  ii.  p.  105.  She  is  said  to  have  lived  to  the  age  of  100  years.

*  The  Debatable  Ground  was  a  tract  of  land  claimed  by  both  kingdoms,  which 
was  the  occasion  of  infinite  troubles  and  vexations.  It  was  in  length  eight  com- 
puted miles  of  the  country,  and  in  breadth  four  miles.  The  subjects  of  both 
kingdoms  commonly  depastured  their  cattle  upon  it  in  the  day-time,  but  were  to 
remove  them  before  sunset  on  the  peril  that  should  ensue.— Cf.  Nicholson  and 
Burn,  i.  p.  16.

*  Aug.  30,  1640.  Od  the  27th  August  the  king  received  intelligence  from  Lord 
Conway  that  the  Scotch  had  invaded  England,  and  would  that  night  be  near 
Newcastle  with  their  army.  On  that  day  the  Scotch  encamped  near  Newbum. 
The  engMgement  took  place  the  next  day,  when  the  king's  forces  were  defeated. 
On  the  29th  Lord  Conway  and  Sir  Jacob  Astlcy  drew  off  their  troops  to  Durham, 
leaving  Newcastle  defenceless.  In  the  afternoon  of  that  day  Sir  Peter 
Riddell,  on  threat  of  bombardment,  opened  the  gates  of  Newcastle  to  the  Scotch. 
On  Monday,  the  31st,  Lesley  came  and  pitched  his  tents  on  Gateshead  Hill,  half  a 
mile  south  of  Newcastle.  Sept.  3.  Gi*eat  alarm  felt  by  the  inhabitants  of  New- 
castle, who  fled  in  great  numbers.  Same  at  Durham. — Rushworth,  Part  II.  vol.  ii. 
p.  1234,  et  seqq.

does  not  occur.  James,  who  looked  to  the  gates,  was  doubtless,  therefore,  one  of 
the  chamberlains,  or  valets-de-chambre,  and  often  designated  probably  by  his 
official  name,  if  we  may  di^^uify  it  by  that  appellation.  Neither  does  any  one

speedily  see  and  disceme  that  it  is  not  in  the  power  of  man  in  earth  to 
wistande  the  holly  will  and  divine  pleasure  of  God  in  heaven,  whoe  ys 
the  Author  of  all  right,  and  fountaine  of  all  justice,  whose  name  be 
ever  more  praysed  and  glorify ed. 

19  Decembris,  A.D.  1605.

and  M'.  Secretarie  Walsingham  bj  her  Majestie's 
commaundement  between  the  Erie  of  Arundell  and 
the  Lord  William  Howard  his  brother,  and  M**. 
Francis  Dacre,  Esquire. 

1.  First,  it  is  ordred  that  the  said  Francis  Dacre,  nor  anie  other  by 
his  meanes,  or  in  his  right,  shall  putt  anie  tenant  out  of  their  posses- 
sion, and  yf  anie  tenant  shall  attume  to  him  and  shall  dye,  the  said 
Francis  shall  putt  in  no  newe  tenant,  but  such  to  have  the  tenure  as 
by  the  Lawe  or  custome  ought  to  succeed. 

2.  Item,  it  is  ordred  yf  anie  delay  shalbe  used  on  the  behalf  of  the 
said  Frauncis  Dacres,  or  anie  other  in  his  right  in  the  tryall  of  the

for  the  ordering  of  the  possession  as  shalbe  thought  convenient. 

3.  Item,  it  is  ordred  that  the  said  Francis  Dacre  nor  anie  other  in 
his  right  shall  use  anie  force  or  forcible  meanes  to  gett  anie  possession 
or  cause  anie  tenant  to  attume,  or  make  or  cause  or  assent  to  anie 
rescous  to  be  made. 

4.  Item,  it  is  ordered  that  all  former  orders  made  by  the  Lords  shall, 
from  the  zj^^  day  of  Aprill  next,  be  void  and  have  no  longer  force. 

5.  Item,  that  all  rents  that  remayne  in  the  hands  eyther  of  the 
Queene's  lleceavors,  the  tenants,  or  anie  others,  heretofore  due,  shalbe 
paied  to  the  Earle  and  Lord  William,  except  the  rent  of  such  tenants 
as  did  atturne  to  the  said  Francis  Dacres  without  compulsion  before 
the  first  order  taken  by  the  Lords,  and  those  rents  so  excepted  to  be 
paid  to  the  said  Francis. 

U.  Item,  yf  anie  force  shalbe  committed  touching  the  premisses  thai 
the  partie  that  is  the  cause  thereof  shall  beare  the  blame.

As  it  hath  pleased  your  Lordship  hetherto  to  extend  your  favour 
towardes  me  in  my  (though  distressed  yet  iust  cause)  so  doe  I  most 
humblie  beseche  your  good  Lordship  as  ever  you  doe  expect  reward 
at  God's  hand  in  releaving  the  cases  of  the  distressed,  to  consider  of 
my  cause  and  my  sincere  carriage  of  my  self  therin,  which  hath  bene 
in  all  dutie  to  hir  Majestic,  and  I  trust  with  such  regard  to  your 
Lordship  and  the  place  you  are  in,  as  I  have  not  in  env  sort  abused 
your  Lordship,  nor  neclected  cny  parte  of  my  duetie,  which  I  assure 
my  self  will  so  fall  owtt  if  it  shall  please  your  Lordship  at  my  humble 
suite  to  vouchsafe  the  examination  thereof.  For  what  hir  Majestic 
is  informed  I  knowe  not.  What  I  have  done  I  am  well  assured  of, 
and  herein  as  before  by  word,  so  nowe  under  my  hand  with  advised 
consideration  I  doe  protest  unto  your  liordship  I  never  neither  by 
letter  or  supplication  writ  unto  hir  Majestic,  nor  by  eny  meanes  made 
eny  offer  unto  hir  concerning  the  title  of  my  land,  other  then  by

present  unto  your  Lordship.  And  nowe  have  presumed  to  offer  the 
trewe  coppie  thereof  to  your  Lordship's  vewe,  most  humblie  beseching 
your  Lordship  to  vouchsafe  the  reading  thereof,  the  which  I  trust 
will  satisfie  your  Lordship  that  I  have  not  so  farre  forgotten  my  self 
as  to  informe  your  Lordship  one  waie  and  underhand  write  an  other 
waie,  as  by  the  practice  of  my  adversaries  it  should  seeme  is  informed 
hir  Majestic,  tending  aswell  to  my  discredit  as  my  utter  undowing.

The  Lord  Willyam  Howard  is  a  knowne  Kecosant,  dwellinge  in  the

plughe,  whose  ladie  is  a  Recusant,  himselfe  in  religion  verie  backward.

Willyam  hath  latelie  married  one  of  lus  sonnes;  the  said  Preston

the  number  of  Recusants  dailie  increaseth  in  those  partes  by  his 
Lordshippe's  countenance.

Memorandum.  The  Countie  of  Cumberland  is  devided  into  fowei 
wardes,  which  in  some  parts  of  the  Kingdome  are  tearmed  Hundreds,

Item,  For  Eske  and  Liddale,  being  solie  in  the  possession  of  the 
£arle  of  Cumberland,  wee  forbeare  to  mention  in  our  certificate,  the

and  therefore  himselfe,  with  such  as  he  pleaseth  to  call  to  joine  with

Item,  For  Allerdale  ward,  Cumberland  ward,  and  Leeth  ward,  they

Right  trustie  and  well  beloved,  Wee  greete  you  well.  Wee  under- 
stand by  our  cosen,  the  Earle  Marshall,  how  careful!  you  have  beene

require  the  continuance  of  your  diligence  and  good  endeavor,  though 
Wee  doubt  not  thereof,  yet  Wee  think  fitt  in  this  speciall  maner  to 
recommend  unto  you  the  carefull  pursuance  of  such  further  direc- 
tions* as  you  shall  from  time  to  time  receive  from  us  or  our  said 
cosen,  which  Wee  shall  graciously  accept.  Given  under  our  signet  at 
Our  Court  at  Oatlands,  the  last  day  of  July,  in  the  fourteenth  yeare 
of  our  raigne,  1638.

The  next  morning  we  happUy  lighted  on  a  guide,  who  by  chance 
was  bound  for  those  intricate  wayes,  a  perfect  intelligencer  was  he, 
and  we  did  imagine  him  to  be  some  processe  carryer,  or  some  mes- 
senger, or  informer,  that  used  to  visit  those  northerne  parts,  for  he 
was  both  perfect  in  the  wayes,  and  the  places  of  the  cheife  men,  in 
those  countryes.  With  him  we  mounted  for  Carlile,  still  along  by 
the  Picts'  wall,  the  wayes  we  found  as  mountainous,  rocky,  and  dan- 
gerous as  those  the  daye  before,  but  not  so  tedious,  in  respect  we  had 
a  good  guide.  Many  ancient  castles  and  seats,  and  some  parkes,  we 
pass'd  by  in  our  sight  on  both  hands,  but  more  especially  (as  we  are 
specially  bound  to  that  house)  wee  did  not  let  passe,  the  stately  and 
fayre  Castle  of  Naworth,  with  that  large,  ston'd  walled  parke,  wherein 
many  beards  of  deere  doe  feed  on  such  high  mountaines  as  com« 
maunds  and  overtops  the  whole  country  thereabouts,  and  some  part 
of  the  next  adiacent  kingdome.  The  parkes,  liberties,  and  forrest, 
that  doth  belong  to  that  noble  old  lord,  all  togeather,  within  the 
compasse  of  his  own  territories,  I  dare  (hearing  the  same  verefy'd 
from  his  Lordship's  owne  mouth)  averre  to  be  as  great  a  quantity 
togeather  in  one  place,  as  any  one  other  Lord  hath  whatsoever. 

Heere  wee  intended  to  tender  our  respects  and  services,  but  his 
late  removall  prevented  our  designe,  onely  we  stay'd  a  little  while  in 
viewing  his  Lordship's  mansion  house,  and  castle,  kingly  hall,  &e. 


488  APPENDIX. 

But  his  Lordship  and  retinue  being  absent,  we  hast'ned  away  for  Gar- 
lile,  but  let  us  (before  we  part  out  of  his  Lordship's  precincts)  not 
forget  to  tell  you  what  lucky  entertainment  wee  met  with  in  a  little 
poore  cottage  in  his  liberties,  driven  in  thither  with  very  ill  weather, 
to  wit,  a  cup  of  nappy  ale,  and  a  peece  of  a  red  deere  pye,  more  then 
we  thought  fit  to  acquaint  his  Lordship  with. 

Not  long  before  we  came  into  his  Lordship's  large  territorise  of 
Gilsland,  we  pass'd  the  Picts'  wall,  which  runs  quite  through  the 
counties  of  Northumberland  and  Cumberland,  begining  at  Walsend, 
neere  the  east  sea,  upon  the  river  of  Tyne,  and  ending  at  the  west 
sea,  a  little  beyond  Carlile,  which  the  Bomane  Emperors  first  made 
8  foot  broad,  and  12  foot  high,  and  80  mile  long,  and  there,  over  a 
little  rivolet,  we  entred  into  the  next  county,  the  place  w^here  the 
High  Sheriffe  receives  the  Judges  with  many  attendant  bonnetts  and 
gallowayes,  and  heere  we  left  Tyne  to  seeke  his  head,  not  far  firom 
Tees.  From  that  place  to  Warwicke  Bridge  we  pass'd  all  the  way 
over  that  Lord's  liberties  and  franchises,  and  then  over  the  river 
Eden,  by  a  fayre  arch't  bridge,  and  to  end  our  second  weeke's  travell, 
passing  the  little  brooke  Petterell,  we  came  safe  and  well,  though  wdl 
wet,  to  our  inne,  the  Angell,  in  the  market  place  in  that  old  strong 
citty  of  Carlile,  built  by  a  British  king  neere  1000  yeeres  hefore 
Christ ;  for  of  these  two  properties,  antiquitie  and  strength,  it  may 
cheifely  boast,  it  being  otherwise,  both  for  revenues,  buildings,  and 
the  inhabitants  and  their  condition,  very  poore. 

The  next  day  we  repayr'd  to  their  Cathedrall,  which  is  nothing  soe 
fayre  and  stately  as  those  we  had  seene,  but  more  like  a  great,  wild 
country  church ;  and  as  it  appeared  outwardly  so  was  it  inwardly, 
neither  beautify'd  nor  adom'd  one  whit.     I  remember  no  more  monu- 
ments of  note  but  that  of  Bishop  Oglethorpe,  that  crowned  our  late 
vertuous  Queene  Elizabeth ;  and  that  of  Snowden,  the  Bishop  that 
preach'd  Robin  Hood  to  our  late  renowned  king.     The  organs  and 
voices  did  well  agree,  the  one  being  Hke  a  shrill  bagpipe,  the  other 
like  the  Scottish  tone.     The  Sermon,  in  the  like  accent,  was  such  as 
wee  would  hardly  bring   away,  though  it  was  delivered  by  a  neat 
young  scholler,  (sent  that  morning  from  Rose  Castle,  the  Bishop *8 
Mansion,  which  stands  upon  Rose   and  Cawd   rivers)   one  of   the 
Bishop's  chaplaines,  to  supply  his  Lord's  place  that  day.     The  Com- 
munion also  was  administred,  and  received  in  a  wild  and  unreverent 
manner. 

To  leave  the  Church  we  made  bold  a  little  with  the  day  to  view 
the  citty,  and  in  it  the  cheife  place,  the  strong  and  fayre  Castle,  built 
by  William  Rufus  upon  a  rocke,  close  by  the  river,  which  comes  from 
Appleby,  on  the  north  side  of  the  citty  towards  Scotland,  over  which 
river  there  is  a  fayre  stone  bridge  of  9  or  10  arches,  about  8  miles 
from  the  sea.  When  we  were  on  the  top  of  the  Castle,  we  easily 
discemM  the  silver  sands  that  in  that  place  part  the  two  kingdomes, 
and  neere  to  them  Burgh  on  the  Sands,  where  King  Edward  the  first 
breathed  his  last ;  Great  Nay  Church  and  Brunswicke  hill  in  Scot- 


APPENDIX.  489 

land  we  at  the  same  time  did  see,  which  sight  did  sufficiently  satisfy 
us,  without  the  cariosity  or  paines  of  travelling  thither. 

This  ancient  citty  hath  felt  much  of  the  feirceness  of  the  hordering 
Scotts,  which  hath  caused  her  to  be  guarded  with  as  strong  and  defen« 
sible  a  wall  and  eittadells  as  any  other  in  England,  through  which 
wee  enter  her  by  three  strong  gates.  It  makes  shift  to  maintaine  a 
Mayor,  distinguished  by  his  white  stafie,  and  12  Aldermen  his 
brethren,  sans  cap  of  maintenance,  but  their  blew  bonnets,  which  they 
are  as  proud  in  as  our  southeme  cittizens  in  their  beavers.  Two  of 
the  Aldermen,  being  very  worthy  knights,  doth  grace  and  coun- 
tenance their  company,  and  poore  citty,  not  a  little,  soe  the  grave 
Recorder  doth,  being  a  knight  also.  [In  marg :  S'.  Bichard  Graham 
and  S'.  George  Dalston.     S'.  Tho.  Carleton,  Recorder.] 

Whilst  we  were  thus  rounding,  facing,  counter-marching,  and 
wheeling,  in  this  strong  garrison  towne,  we  heard  of  a  messenger 
from  that  truly  noble  Lord  we  the  last  day  missed  on  at  Naworth, 
with  a  curteons  invitation  to  dinner  at  Corby  Castle  the  next  day, 
(for  there  his  Lordship  then  was)  which  we  accompted  (as  it  was 
indeed)  a  mighty  favour  from  soe  noble  a  person,  and  sent  backe 
his  Lordship's  servant  with  the  tender  of  our  services  till  the  next 
day,  that  we  were  to  wayte  upon  his  Lordship  to  present  them  our 
selves. 

The  next  day  wee  went  thither,  and  were  by  that  generous  brave 
Lord  curteously  and  nobly  entertayn'd,  and  sony,  he  sayd,  he  was, 
that  hee  was  not  at  Naworth  to  give  us  then  the  like.  His  Lord- 
ship's commaunds  made  us  to  transgresse  good  manners,  for  neither 
would  he  su£Per  us  to  speake  uncovered,  nor  to  stand  up  (although 
our  duty  required  another  posture)  but  plac'd  us  by  his  LordBhip  him- 
selfe  to  discourse  with  him  imtill  dinner  time. 

Anon  appeared  a  grave  and  vertuous  matron,  his  Honorable  Lady, 
who  told  us,  indeed  we  were  heartily  welcome,  and  whilst  our  Ancient 
and  my  selfe  addressed  our  selves  to  satisfy  his  Lordship  in  such 
occurrences  of  Norfolke  as  he  pleas'd  to  aske,  and  desir'd  to  know, 
wee  lefb  our  modest  Captaine  to  relate  to  his  noble  Lady  what  she 
desir'd.  These  noble  twaine  (as  it  pleas'd  themselves  to  tell  us 
themselves)  could  nott  make  above  25  yeeres  both  togeather,  when 
first  they  were  marry *d,  that  now  can  make  above  140  yeares,  and 
are  very  hearty,  well,  and  merry,  and  long  may  they  continue  soe, 
for  soe  have  they  all  iust  cause  to  pray,  that  live  neere  them,  for 
their  hospitality  and  fre  entertainment,  agrees  with  their  generous 
and  noble  extraction,  and  their  yeeres  retaines  the  memory  of  their 
honorable  predecessors'  bountifuU  house  keeping. 

Amongst  other  dishes  that  came  then  to  his  Lordship's  table,  one 
there  was  serv'd  in  at  the  second  course,  which  was  not  usuall,  a  live 
roe  ;*  and  as  there  was  great  store  of  venison,  soe  was  there  plenty  of

A. 

Mh.  Nicholas  Roscaeeock.^ 

The  name  of  Mr.  Koscarrock  occurs  very  frequently  in  the  House- 
hold Books  of  Naworth  Castle,  which  seems  to  have  been  his  home 
from  the  year  1607,  if  not  before,  until  his  death.  (See  ante,  pp.  6, 
7,  n.)  Nicholas  Roscarrock  was  the  fifbh  son  of  Richard  Roscarrock, 
Esquire,  of  Roscarrock,  by  Isabella,  daughter  of  Richard  Trevenor, 
and  heir  of  her  brother,  William  Trevenor.  His  father,  during  his  life- 
time, settled  upon  him  the  estates  of  Penhale,  Carbura,  and  Newton, 
in  the  parishes  of  St.  Cleer  and  St  German's,  in  Cornwall.  (See  Sir  J. 
Maclean's  History  of  Trigg  Minor y  i  558.)  "  His  industrious  delight 
in  matters  of  history  and  antiquity,"  which  Carew  makes  mention  of, 
is  corroborated  from  other  sources  of  information.  In  1572  there  was 
published  by  Richard  Tottell,  "the  Workes  of  Armories  deuyded  into 

three  bookes collected  and  gathered  by  John  Bossewell, 

Gentleman."  To  this  work  is  prefixed  a  long  set  of  verses  (ninety- 
four  in  all),  signed  "Nicolas  Roscarrocke."  They  bear  the  fantastic 
title  of  "  Cilenus'  censure  of  the  aucthor  in  his  high  court  of 
Herehaultry."  Bossewell's  book* was  reprinted  in  1597,  and  to  this 
edition  Roscarrock's  verses,  but  with  some  varieties  in  spelling,  were 
again  prefixed.  In  1576  there  appeared  "  The  Steele  OlaSy  a  satyre 
compiled  by  George  Gascoigne,  Esquire,  ....  printed  for 
Richard  Smith."  Amongst  the  verses  with  which  this  satire  was 
ushered  into  the  world  was  a  set  entitled  "  N.  R.  in  commendation  of 
the  author  and  his  workes ;"  and  there  can  be  little  doubt  but  that 
N.R.  stands  for  Nicholas  Roscarrock.     He  was  at  this  time  a  member

vol.  iv.,  p.  402.

Mr.  Roscarrock  was  a  zealous  Catholic.  In  1577  the  laws  against 
recusants  were  put  in  force  in  Cornwall,  when  his  name  appears 
amongst  those  who  suffered.  He  was  accused  at  the  Launceston 
Assizes  (16**»  Sept.  1677),  "for  not  going  to  the  church"  (Morris* 
Troubles  of  our  Catholic  Forefathers,  p.  95).  In  London,  a  few  years 
after,  his  opposition  to  the  Government  assumed  a  more  active  form. 
He  became  a  member  of  the  Toung  Men's  Club  that  was  formed  in 
1580  for  helping  the  Missionary  priests,  and  solemnly  blessed  by  the 
Pope.  George  Gilbert,  a  great  patron  and  supporter  of  the  Catholics, 
often  stopped  with  **y«  ij  Roscarochs"  (Jesuits  in  Conflict ,  p.  206). 
Ralph  Sherwin,  executed  in  1581,  was  taken  in  Roscarrock's  chamber, 


with  the  following  note : — "  I  received  this  morning  a  ston  from  my  Lord  of 
Arandol,  sent  him  m>m  my  Lord  William.  It  was  the  head  of  a  cross  at  Bewcastle." 
The  ornamentation  of  the  monolith  is  varied,  interlacing,  chequer-work  (which  it 
is  almost  needless  to  say  has  nothing  to  do  with  the  arms  of  Vanx),  and  a  fToit- 
bearing  tree,  ascending  in  curved  lines,  with  foliage  and  clusters,  from  the  lower 
part  of  the  pillar.  There  are  also  figures  in  low  relief  on  one  side,  the  most 
prominent  being  one  of  our  Blessed  Lord  in  the  attitude  of  benediction.  The 
lowest  figure  is  that  of  a  man  bearing  a  hawk.  Mr.  Stephens  (Old  Northern 
Runic  Monuments  of  Scandinavia  and  JSngland,  ^c,  Vol.  I.,  pp.  398  et  seqq.)  gives 
an  elaborate  interpretation  of  the  Runes  engraven  on  the  Cross,  and  tells  us  that 
they  indicate  that  it  was  erected  in  memory  of  Alcfrith,  who  was  raised  by  his 
father  Oswi  (the  Sovereign  of  all  Northumbria)  to  be  king  of  Deira.  Alcfrith  was 
a  pious  and  brave  prince,  and  a  friend  of  St.  Wilfrid.  As  the  inscription  indicates 
(in  Mr.  Stephens'  opinion)  that  the  monument  was  not  finished  till  the  first  year  of 
Kcgfrith,  his  successor,  the  date  he  assigns  to  it  is  about  670.  It  bears  a  great 
resemblance  to  the  very  interesting  and  perfect  cross  at  Buthwell  in  Dumfriesshire.

shewn  themselves  braver  than  many  priests.'*     {Stonyhurst  MS 8.  P. 
fol.  39,  quoted   in   the   Life  of  Father  Weston,  ed.   Father  John 
Morris.) 

Mention  is  made  of  him,  also,  in  one  of  Walsingham*s  "  Secret 
Advertisements  *'  (P.  R.  O.  Elizabeth,  vol.  clxxviii.  n.  11),  dated 
April  6,  1585,  which  gives  the  following  relation  : — "  Sithence  my  last

prisoner  in  the  Tower,  concerning  Crichton,  the  Scottish  Jesuit  there, 
viz.,  whether  he  had  any  means  to  confer  with  his  friends,  or  to  convey 
any  letters  unto  them  sithence  his  committing  to  the  Tower.  He 
answered  me  that  when  Crichton  was  first  committed,  he  was  lodged 
in  Martin  Tower,  right  over  the  lodging  of  Nicholas  Roscarrock, 
which  said  Nicholas  did  oftentimes  by  some  device  open  two  doors 
which  were  between  their  lodgings,  and  so  they  conferred  at  pleasure, 
and  also  the  said  Pierrepont  said  unto  me  that  such  letters  as  Crichton 
did  write,  were  by  the  said  Nicholas  conveyed  out  of  his  chamber 
window,  which  was  near  the  ground,  to  a  little  maiden  which  was  sent 
often  to  him  from  Orton,  which  was  late  banished,  and  so  by  him 
farther  conveyed  out  of  the  Tower,  but  to  whom  or  what  place  he 
seemed  ignorant ;  only  some  of  them  were  conveyed  to  the  Lord  Gray, 
that  not  long  sithence  was  Ambassador  from  Scotland  during   his 

abode  here  in  England It  seemeth  that  Pierrepont  was 

lodged  where  Crichton  was,  in  Martin  Tower,  and  that  he  had  the 
same  means  to  confer  with  Roscarrock  as  Crichton  had.  My 
acquaintance  is  yet  but  new  with  Pierrepont."  (Life  of  Father 
Weston,  pp.  79,  80.)

five  years  a  prisoner,  and  in  debt  to  the  Lieutenant-Governor  to  140^.

What  originally  brought  Mr.  Roscarrock  and  Lord  William  Howard 
into  the  intimate  relations  which  subsisted  between  them  we  know 
not.  The  similarity  of  their  literary  tastes  and  pursuits,  and  sympathy 
on  the  part  of  Lord  William  for  one  who  had  undergone  cruel  suffer- 
ing for  his  attachment  to  the  ancient  faith,  were  probably  both  com- 
bined. But  he  was  not  a  pensioner  upon  Lord  William's  bounty,  for 
he  evidently  had  means  of  his  own,  derived  no  doubt  from  the  estates 
settled  upon  him  by  his  father.  We  find  him  receiving  interest  from 
Lord  William  upon  money  which  had  been  advanced  by  him  to  the 
latter.  (See  ante,  p.  302.)  In  his  latter  years  his  eyesight  failed, 
but  his  love  of  books  continued  unabated,  as  we  learn  from  a  letter 
written  by  Lord  William  to  Sir  Robert  Cotton  (p.  451),  asking  for 
the  loan  of  a  book  fur  his  old  friend,  who  "  though  he  cannot  take  a 
viewe  therof  yett  he  much  longeth  to  lend  his  eare  to  herken  to  the 
reading  of  the  same.'*  Mr.  Roscarrock  died  at  Naworth,  as  has  been 
stated  above,  in  1633  or  1634.    (See  p.  303.)

ElBKOSWALD   CaSTLB. 
ElTEACTS   PBOM  A  PaPEB  ON  KiBKOSWALD   CaSTLE,   BY   MiCHAEL 

W.  Tatloe,  M.D.y  Penbith.  [Transactions  of  the  Cumber-

Part  I.,  Vol.  II.,  pp.  6, 10.] 

The  site,  which  is  on  slightly  rising  ground,  about  a  quarter  of  a 
mile  to  the  south-east  of  the  village,  presents  no  natural  advantages  as 
a  defensive  position.  The  approach  is  by  an  ancient  causeway,  which 
runs  parallel  with,  and  close  to  the  counterscarp  of  the  moat,  on  its 
western  border.  The  moat  encompasses  a  level  area  of  about  one 
and  three-quarter  acres,  nearly  in  the   centre  of  which  stands  the 

fortress The  fosse  is  of  a  rectangular  figure,  exactly  following 

the  contour  of  the  castle,  and  surrounding  it  on  every  side.  In  one 
direction  it  is  380  feet  long,  in  the  other  300  feet ;  inside  measure- 
ments. It  has  an  average  width  of  30  or  40  feet,  and  might  have 
had  a  depth  of  from  12  to  18  feet ;  it  was  supplied  with  water  by  a 
brook  from  the  ponds  in  the  park  above,  and  when  filled  must  have 
proved  a  very  formidable  obstacle  to  any  assailants.  At  the  western 
angle  of  the  moat  there  is  an  additional  work  of  defence,  of  great 
interest  and  importance ;  it  is  a  rectangular  mound,  an  outwork  or 
ravelin  lying  within  the  moat,  and  provided  with  a  ditch  of  its  own. 
It  is  nearly  square,  the  dimensions  are  45  feet  by  40  feet ;  it  is  on  the 
same  level  as  the  inner  enclosure,  and  the  sides  presented  to  the 
exterior  are  nearly  flush  with  the  lines  of  scarp  of  the  main  ditch. 
The  function  of  this  earthwork  has  been  to  flank  the  main  entrance 
and  drawbridge,  which  probably  were  placed  where  the  gap  now  is, 
about  the  middle  of  the  western  side.  There  remain  no  traces  of 
buildings  of  gatehouse,  or  of  gatehouse  towers,  or  of  barbican,  and 
there  may  have  been  none,  except  the  timber  apparatus  for  the  draw- 
bridge— there  has  been  no  masonry  along  the  edge  of  the  moat,  the 
defence  has  been  by  wooden  stockading. 

The  plan  of  the  castle  seems  to  have  been  quadrangular,  forming  a 
square  of  about  150  feet,  yet  not  regular  nor  complete,  seeing  that  the 
eastern  line  re-enters  at  an  angle,  at  the  southern  comer,  leaving  there 
a  rectangular  recess. 

Two  towers,  of  which  a  good  deal  still  remains,  though  plundered  of 
their  facing-stones,  cap  the  angles  on  the  south  face.  They  are 
nearly  of  the  same  size  and  pattern  and  nearly  square,  35  by  30  feet ; 
they  are  about  50  feet  apart,  and  set  on  nearly  flush  with  the  curtain 
wall  which  has  connected  them.  They  have  had  a  basement,  and  a 
first  and  second  floor.  The  basement  in  each  consists  of  a  vaulted 
chamber,  entered  from  the  ward,  at  the  court  level,  by  a  narrow  door- 
way with  a  pointed  arch,  and  plainly  chamfered  ;  each  is  lighted  with

ADDENDA.  513 

This  hall,  if  we  rely  on  history  and  tradition,  cannot  have  been 
exceeded  in  baronial  magnificence,  and  in  the  splendour  of  its  internal 
decoration,  by  any  existing  in  our  counties  in  the  sixteenth  century. 
We  may  consider  the  hall,  and  the  buildings  connected  with  it,  and 
the  staircase  tower,  to  have  constituted  the  additions  made  to  the 
castle  about  the  year  1600. 

Sandford,  who  visited  this  place  about  1610,  says  in  his  MSS., 
**  this  great  castle  of  Kirkoswald  was  once  the  fairest  fabric  that  ever 
eyes  looked  upon.  The  hall  1  have  seen,  100  feet  long ;  and  the 
great  portraiture  of  King  Brute  lying  in  the  end  of  the  roof  of  this 
hall,  and  of  all  his  succeeding  successors  Kings  of  England  portraicted 
to  the  waist,  their  visage,  hats,  feathers,  garbs,  and  habits,  in  the  roof 
of  this  hall ;  now  translated  to  Naward  Castle,  where  they  are  placed 
in  the  roof  of  the  hall,  and  at  the  end  thereof.  This  castle  was  the 
ancient  palace  of  the  Lord  Multon,  marrying  the  Lord  Vaux's  heir, 
lord  of  Naworth  and  Gilsland ;  and  afterwards  of  the  late  Lords 
Dacre  ;  and  now  come  by  lineal  descent  to  the  tresgallant  the  Earls 
of  Sussex ;  with  the  lands  adjoining,  and  many  brave  parks  and  villages 

belonging  thereto." 

•  ••••• 

Let  us  now  turn  to  the  western  face,  or  frbnt  of  the  enceinte. 
Amid  the  hillocks,  and  hollows,  and  heaps  of  grass-grown  rubbish, 
that  encumber  this  side  of  the  ruin,  it  is  possible  to  indicate  the  site 
of  the  gateway  as  having  consisted  of  an  outer  and  inner  gate, 
flanked  with  turrets,  or  tower-like  buttresses.  It  was  usual  in  the 
outer  bailey,  outside  of  the  walls,  to  have  the  stabling,  out-offices, 
and  inferior  apartments — the  site  of  these  may  be  traced  in  the 
foundation  of  main  walls  and  partitions,  covered  by  the  turf,  ex- 
tending from  the  northern  boundary  of  the  castle  to  the  scarp  of  the 
moat. 

It  is  possible  that  the  road  of  approach  to  the  castle  gate,  from 
the  drawbridge  and  the  moat,  was  sunken  below  the  level  of  the 
ground,  in  the  manner  of  a  trench  or  covered  way,  so  as  to  shelter 
the  advance  or  retreat  of  the  defenders  ;  the  depression  in  the  ground 
suggests  the  idea. 

•  ••••• 

To  sum  up  what  can  be  told  of  the  antiquity  of  Kirkoswald  Castle. 
I  would  say — there  is  no  part  of  it  to  which  an  earlier  date  can  be 
assigned  than  the  beginning  of  the  fourteenth  century.  The  inceptive 
work  of  Randolph  Engain  has  been  of  no  account, — the  Norman  has 
left  no  mark  here — there  is  no  single  massive  keep  nor  citadel, — 
the  invariable  characteristic  of  the  strong  Norman  fortress,  and 
which  we  find  abiding  almost  in  its  pristine  strength,  when  the 
adjacent  buildings  of  a  subsequent  date  are  mouldering  in  ruins. 

The  two  original  towers  afford  the  key  to  its  design  and  pro- 
portions, as  a  small  Edwardian  Castle,  that  is,  a  quadrangular  mural 
enclosure,  with  projecting  towers  capping  the  angles.

%*  The  earlier  descents  in  the  above  genealogy  as  given  in  the  Kirkos- 
wald  window,  are  inaccurate,  possibly  apocryphal.  The  interments 
of  Humphrey,  Richard,  and  William,  are  said  to  have  taken  place 
at  Holbeach.  But  this  must  be  a  misstatement.  The  Manor  of 
Holbeach  did  not  come  into  the  hands  of  the  Dacres  until  the 
marriage  of  Randolph  Dacre  with  Margaret,  daughter  and  heir  of 
Thomas  de  Multon.  The  Dacres  had  no  previous  connexion  with 
Lincolnshire.  The  following  is  an  abridged  account  of  their  descent, 
as  given  by  Dugdale  (Baronage,  vol.  ii.  p.  22): — 

1.  William  de  Dacre,  of  Dacre,  co.  Cumberland,  was  Sheriff  of  Cumber- 
land, 20  Hen.  III. ;  Sheriff  of  Yorkshire,  32  Hen.  III.,  and  Governor  of 
Carlisle  by  patent  62  Hen.  III.,  in  which  year  he  died. 

2.  Ranulph,  son  and  heir,  succeeded  his  father  as  Sheriff  of  Cumber- 
land and  Governor  of  Carlisle.  He  died  1-1  Edward  I.  By  his  wife 
Joane,  daughter  of  Lady  Alice  de  Lucy,  he  had  a  son  and  heir, — 

3.  William,  who  was  20  years  of  age  in  14  Edw.  I.  In  1  Edw.  II.  he 
had  a  licence  to  castellute  his  house  at  Dunwalloght,  co.  Cumb.  He  was 
summoned  to  Parliament  from  28  Edw.  I.  until  12  Edw.  II.  inclusive. 
He  married  Joane,  heir  of  Benedict  Gernet,  in  whose  right  he  became 
possessed  of  Halton,  Pishwicke,  and  Eccleston,  co.  Lane.  She  survived 
her  husband.    By  her  he  had  a  son  and  heir, — 

4.  Ranulph,  Sheriff  of  Cumb.,  4  Edw.  III.,  and  Governor  of  Carlisle. 
In  9  Edw.  III.  he  obtained  a  licence  to  castellate  his  house  at  Naworth. 
He  married  Margaret,  daughter  and  heir  of  Thomas  de  Multon,  Lord  of 
Gilsland.  Ranulph  died  13  Edw.  III.,  and  was  succeeded  by  his  eldest 
son  and  heir, — 

5.  William,  who  was  20  years  old  at  his  father's  death.  He  died 
33  Edw.  III.  s.  p.,  being  seised  of  the  Manor  of  Holbeach  in  Lincolnshire, 
2  parts  of  the  Manor  of  Dacre,  the  Manors  of  Fishwicke,  Halton,  and 
Eccleston,  co.  Lane,  and  the  Manor  of  Nether  Tralyng  in  Roxburghshire, 
and  was  sucr.eeded  by  his  next  brother, — 

6.  Ranulph,  who  was  in  Holy  Orders,  and  Rector  of  Prestecotes.  He 
died  49  Edw.  III.,  and  was  succeeded  by  his  brother  and  next  heir, — 

7.  Hugh,  who  was  summoned  to  Parliament  from  50  Edw.  III.  until 
5  Ric.  II.     He  died  7  Ric.  II.,  leaving  a  son  and  heir, — 

8.  William,  who  was  26  years  old  at  his  father's  death.  He  was 
summoned  to  Parliament  from  7  Ric.  II.  until  22  Ric.  II.  He  died  20 
July,  22  Ric.  II.,  and  was  succeeded  by  his  son  and  heir, —
